title: The Long Delayed Echoes
subtitle: Oslo, Norway · 1927
voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.
grade: Muted documentary still, a 1920s Norwegian amateur radio operator's world at night, warm amber valve-glow against deep cold blue-black night, quiet, lonely and uncanny, cinematic vertical composition with one centred subject, fine film grain. Single image, not a collage, no text, no lettering, no numbers on dials, no people, no faces, no hands.

beats.vo: Oslo, nineteen twenty-seven. A Dutch radio signal arrived, then arrived again, three seconds later.
beats.img: Close view of a 1920s home-built shortwave radio receiver filling most of the width of the frame: a dark polished wooden cabinet with three glowing vacuum valves standing on top and two plain round black dials on its front, a pair of old headphones resting beside it, centred on a worn wooden desk, the warm amber glow of the valves lighting the wood and dials brightly so the set reads clearly at small size, a frosted window with deep blue night softly out of focus behind, no people, no hands, no lettering, no numbers, no markings.

beats.vo: Radio circles the Earth in a seventh of a second. The cause is still unknown.
beats.img: A single long wire radio aerial strung between two tall wooden poles on a snowy hillside above a dark Norwegian fjord at night, centred in the frame, the wire faintly catching cold light, a vast clear starry night sky above, dark water and dark hills below, quiet and still, no aurora, no people, no buildings, no lettering.

facts.claim: In 1927 (end of summer), Jørgen Hals, a Norwegian civil engineer and radio amateur, at his home near Oslo, listening to the Dutch shortwave station PCJJ at Eindhoven, heard besides the principal signal a weaker echo about three seconds later ('A Dutch radio signal arrived, then arrived again, three seconds later'; 'OSLO · 1927')

The usual radio echo goes round the Earth in about 1/7 of a second (Hals: 'the usual echo, which goes round the earth with an interval of about 1/7 second'); light/radio travels ~300,000 km/s and the Earth's circumference is ~40,000 km = ~0.13 s

(caption) Hals wrote to physicist Carl Størmer; Størmer's account appeared in Nature in 1928; Balthasar van der Pol arranged test transmissions from PCJJ with the Oslo group from early 1928, and echoes were observed, e.g. on 11 October 1928 simultaneously in Oslo and Eindhoven
(caption) Long delayed echoes have been heard sporadically from 1927 up to the present day; proposed explanations include ionospheric/magnetospheric ducting and mode conversion, none confirmed

Still unexplained as of 2026: Space.com (Micah Hanks, 27 Oct 2026) 'The exact cause of this unusual phenomenon ... remains unknown'; Sverre Holm (University of Oslo): LDEs are 'still not properly explained'; Wikipedia lists LDE under unsolved problems in physics
